extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and scholars of English common law
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains foundational doctrines and categories of the laws of England, especially the absolute rights of persons and the historical/administrative context of jurisdictions. Aimed at understanding legal principles and their historical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Township/tithing/hamlet definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Towns originally contained one parish and one tithing; hamlets are small appendages. Sir Henry Spelman conjectures an entire vill consisted of ten freemen, demi-vills of five, and hamlets of less than five.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These small collections of houses sometimes share administration with the town or have separate officers; when separate they may be treated as distinct townships for some legal purposes (statute of Exeter references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hundred (and wapentake) definition and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: A hundred consists of ten tithings (ten times ten families) and is governed by a high constable or bailiff; historically the hundred court met there though now fallen into disuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some northern counties hundreds are called wapentakes. The hundred is a unit for local government and local justice under historic common law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and function of hundreds/traditional continental analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: The subdivision into hundreds (and tithings) is ancient and found in Denmark and among the Franks/Germans: districts of a hundred freemen under a centenarius, subject to a comes (count).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These divisions were both military and civil and were intended to hold each district answerable for robberies committed within it; the institution traces to ancient Germanic practices (Tacitus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shire/county and sheriff role
rubrics_metrics.description: A shire (county) is an indefinite number of hundreds; 'county' (comitatus) derives from comes (count/earl). The sheriff (vice-comes, shire-reeve) is the chief local officer and exercises civil administration by process of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some counties have intermediate divisions (lathes in Kent, rapes in Sussex, trithings/ridings) with their own subordinate officers; the number of counties has varied historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counties palatine: definition and palatine privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Counties palatine (e.g., Chester, Durham, Lancaster) are called 'a palatio' because their owners had jura regalia nearly as the king has in his palace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners could pardon treasons, murders and felonies; appoint judges and justices of the peace; have writs and indictments run in their names; offences were against their peace rather than the king's. Many privileges were later abridged by statute, and some palatinates were abolished.

rubrics_metrics.name: County corporate
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain cities and towns were granted the status of counties of themselves (counties corporate) with their own sheriffs and magistrates and not subject to the county at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include London, York, Bristol, Norwich, Coventry; the grant is out of royal favour and modifies the exercise of county authority within those places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of distributing legal subjects: primary division
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of the laws of England are distributed under the heads of RIGHTS and WRONGS for perspicuity and methodical treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone proposes avoiding divisions that are too large or too minute; this primary bifurcation guides the structure of the Commentaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold division of legal objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws are divided into: (1) rights of persons; (2) rights of things; (3) private wrongs (civil injuries) with means of redress; (4) public wrongs (crimes/misdemeanors) with means of prevention and punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fourfold scheme structures the whole commentary and indicates the principal concerns of municipal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between rights and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights are those belonging to a person; duties are what are due from every citizen. Many social duties are relative and thus can be considered as rights due to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: allegiance is usually considered a duty of the people, protection a duty of the magistrate; yet they are reciprocally rights and duties of each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural persons vs artificial persons (corporations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural persons are human beings; artificial persons are created by law for social/government purposes and called corporations or bodies politic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction determines how the law attributes rights and duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute vs relative rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute rights appertain to persons merely as individuals (would exist in a state of nature); relative rights arise from social relations and connexions as members of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute rights are fewer and simpler; relative rights are more numerous and complex and occupy more space in legal codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim of municipal law: protection of absolute rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary end of human laws is to maintain and regulate absolute rights of individuals (those vested by immutable laws of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws also regulate relative rights, but protection of absolute rights is the principal view and should precede other legal concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural liberty vs civil (political) liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural liberty is the power of acting as one thinks fit unless restrained by the law of nature; civil liberty is that natural liberty restrained by human laws only so far as necessary and expedient for the public advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive or causeless restraints by law are tyranny; prudent laws that yield public advantage can enhance civil liberty by securing the social order (Locke cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for valid or legitimate laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws are legitimate when they restrain private will only for public advantage; laws regulating matters of indifference without public utility are oppressive and destructive of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: Edward IV's statute regulating shoe pikes (oppressive) vs Charles II's woollen burial statute (supports national trade and is consistent with public liberty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational statutes declaring English liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: Key historical instruments: Magna Carta, Confirmatio Cartarum, numerous corroborating statutes, Petition of Right, Habeas Corpus Act, Bill of Rights (1688), Act of Settlement — together declare and secure the rights and liberties of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These instruments are treated as declaratory and corroborative of fundamental common law rights; they form the statutory backbone for many liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principal civil immunities
rubrics_metrics.description: The private immunities constituting English rights are reducible to three principal articles: (1) the right of personal security; (2) the right of personal liberty; (3) the right of private property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because compulsion or abridgement of will can only occur by infringing life/member, liberty, or property, preservation of these rights secures civil immunities broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of personal security (components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal security consists in legal and uninterrupted enjoyment of life, limbs, body, health, and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary treats life and limbs as highest value; lesser protections (health, reputation) are acknowledged and later addressed under personal wrongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal beginning of life standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Life, in contemplation of law, begins as soon as an infant is able to stir in the mother's womb (quickening).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, causing death of a quick child in utero was homicide or manslaughter; Blackstone notes the older view and its evolution to lesser characterization (heinous misdemeanour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-defence and pardon of homicide se defendendo
rubrics_metrics.description: Homicide committed in self-defence (se defendendo) is pardoned; acts done to save life or member are considered performed under highest necessity and compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts executed under well-grounded apprehension of losing life or limbs are void if forced; the law recognizes duress as an excuse in many circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duress: types and legal threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Duress is of two sorts: duress of imprisonment (actual loss of liberty) and duress per minas (threatened hardship). Duress per minas is confined to fear of loss of life or mayhem; fear of battery or of property loss is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fear must be such as would affect a resolute person ('that which may fall upon a man constant'); lesser fears (battery, burning house, loss of goods) are not duress because adequate legal remedies (damages) can be had.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for necessities: poor relief as legal duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The law furnishes the indigent with supplies sufficient for necessities of life by statutes for relief of the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone contrasts humane English provision with Roman law reluctance; such statutory reliefs (e.g., foundling hospitals) are part of law's duty to preserve life/member.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil death doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil death occurs when a person is banished from the realm or enters religion (becomes a professed monk); the person is dead in law and his heir takes his estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A civiliter mortuus cannot enjoy secular benefits; executors/administrators may be appointed and acts/conveyances for life usually mean 'natural life' to avoid problems created by civil death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on punishments affecting life or limb and Magna Carta protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution and statute law forbid arbitrary destruction of life or limb; punishments extending to life or limb are inflicted rarely and only upon highest necessity, and no man shall be destroyed except by legal judgment of his peers or the law of the land (Magna Carta).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes (5 Edw. III c.9; 28 Ed. III c.3) reiterate that no man shall be forejudged of life or limb contrary to the great charter and law, and no man shall be put to death without due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of personal liberty and procedural safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal liberty is the power of locomotion and removal of one's person without imprisonment or restraint except by due course of law; no freeman shall be taken or imprisoned except by lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes (Petition of Right; habeas corpus provisions; 31 Car. II c.2 cited) protect against imprisonment by suggestion/petition to the king or by illegal courts and provide for counsel and writs of habeas corpus to test legality of commitment.
